mainTopic: מפקיר נזקיו: whether one who gives up ownership of his dangerous property is liable, and which of רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר holds which view
overview: רבי יוחנן says the dispute about someone whose jug broke in the street is about damage done after the fall. The גמרא shows from another statement of רבי יוחנן that there is a dispute at the moment of the fall too. So his real point is that the רבנן exempt only because the owner was an אנוס, while an ordinary מפקיר נזקיו is liable. Next the גמרא brings a dispute between רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר about whether a מפקיר נזקיו is liable, and works out who holds which side. First it proves that רבי אלעזר says liable, defends that against his ruling about turning over dung (רב אשי: the dung was turned below three טפחים), and concludes that רבי יוחנן says exempt. That conclusion is challenged from the thorn-fence משנה, which the גמרא answers, and then from an unnamed משנה about a pit in רשות הרבים. This second challenge forces the גמרא to reverse itself: רבי יוחנן says liable. The amud ends by asking whether רבי אלעזר must then say exempt, with his statement continuing on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן places the dispute after the fall
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the מחלוקת is about damage that happened after the fall.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: the disagreement is about after the fall.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives his opinion about which stage of the jug-breaking case the dispute covers. He says it covers damage that happened after the jug already fell and broke.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is someone whose jug broke in the public street, and later the water or shards hurt someone. רבי יוחנן says the argument is about damage after the fall. This sounds like a contrast with the moment of the fall itself, which sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: after the fall: the shards or water are already lying in the street
at the time of the fall: damage done as the jug is falling

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan says:
The dispute is about after the fall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an opinion that differs from the view stated earlier in the sugya about the timing of the dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dispute applies to damage that happened after the fall.

steps.title: If everyone exempts at the time of the fall, that clashes with רבי יוחנן later
steps.stepSummary: Maybe רבי יוחנן means everyone exempts at the moment of the fall. But later he implies that רבי מאיר holds one who stumbles is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: But at the time of the fall, what? Everyone agrees he is exempt? But רבי יוחנן says later: 'Do not say our משנה follows רבי מאיר, who says one who stumbles is negligent.' This shows that רבי מאיר makes him liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what רבי יוחנן holds about the moment of the fall. It tries out the reading 'everyone exempts' and then attacks it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might read רבי יוחנן as saying that at the moment of the fall, everyone agrees the owner is exempt. But elsewhere רבי יוחנן himself says רבי מאיר calls a stumbler פושע, which means רבי מאיר would hold him liable. So it cannot be that everyone exempts.

keyTerms.meaning: by inference, it follows from this
later on, further in the גמרא

phrases.english: But at the time of the fall, what?
Everyone agrees he is exempt?
But from the fact that Rabbi Yoḥanan says later:
phrases.notes: 'Later' means on 31a, where he discusses a different משנה in this פרק.

phrases.aramaic: לָא תֵּימָא מַתְנִיתִין רַבִּי מֵאִיר הִיא,
phrases.english: Do not say the mishna is Rabbi Meir,
who says one who stumbles is negligent;
by inference, Rabbi Meir deems him liable!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests one possible reading of רבי יוחנן's statement.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that at the moment of the fall everyone exempts.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן elsewhere says רבי מאיר calls a stumbler negligent, so רבי מאיר holds him liable. That means not everyone exempts.

steps.title: If everyone obligates at the time of the fall, that also clashes
steps.stepSummary: Maybe instead everyone holds him liable at the moment of the fall. But the same later statement shows the רבנן exempt a stumbler.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather what, everyone agrees he is liable? But from the fact that רבי יוחנן says later, 'Do not say our משנה follows רבי מאיר, who says one who stumbles is negligent,' it follows that the רבנן exempt him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the opposite reading, that everyone obligates at the moment of the fall. It knocks this down with the same later statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If only רבי מאיר calls a stumbler negligent, then the רבנן must disagree and exempt him. So 'everyone obligates' fails too. Both simple readings collapse, which pushes the גמרא to find another meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: rather, what then? It tries the other option

phrases.english: Rather, what?
Everyone agrees he is liable?
But from the fact that Rabbi Yoḥanan says later:

phrases.aramaic: לָא תֵּימָא מַתְנִיתִין רַבִּי מֵאִיר הִיא,
phrases.english: Do not say the mishna is Rabbi Meir,
who says one who stumbles is negligent;
by inference, the Rabbis exempt him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries the opposite reading after the first one failed, and rejects it with the same source.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that at the moment of the fall everyone obligates.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If only רבי מאיר calls a stumbler negligent, the רבנן must exempt him. So not everyone obligates.
steps.confusionAlert: The same quote from רבי יוחנן is used twice for opposite purposes. First it shows that רבי מאיר obligates, then it shows that the רבנן exempt. Together they show there IS a dispute at the moment of the fall.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's real point about מפקיר נזקיו
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's lesson is that the רבנן exempt only here, because the owner was an אנוס. In general, one who abandons his dangerous property is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what he teaches us: the רבנן exempt one who abandons his damaging property only here, because he is an אנוס. But one who abandons his damaging property in general, they hold liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what רבי יוחנן was really coming to teach. The dispute exists at the moment of the fall too, and his point is about why the רבנן exempt even after the fall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the fall, the owner has given up ownership of the shards, so he is a מפקיר נזקיו. The רבנן exempt him only because the jug broke by accident, so he is an אנוס. In an ordinary case where someone abandons a dangerous item, even the רבנן hold him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what he teaches us
one who gives up ownership of his property that causes damage
someone who could not help what happened

steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן exempt the jug owner only because he was an אנוס. Giving up ownership of a dangerous item does not, by itself, free a person from paying.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a broad rule: in ordinary cases, a מפקיר נזקיו is liable for the damage his abandoned property causes. The exemption here is a special exception because the owner was an אנוס.

phrases.english: Rather, this is what he teaches us:
that one who renounces ownership of his hazardous property here,
it is he whom the Rabbis exempt,
because he is a victim of circumstances beyond his control;
but one who renounces his hazardous property in general,
they deem liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles both challenges by giving רבי יוחנן's statement a new purpose.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the purpose of the statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רבי יוחנן meant that at the moment of the fall there is no dispute.
steps.terutzMaskana: There is a dispute at the moment of the fall too. רבי יוחנן's point is that the רבנן exempt after the fall only because the owner was an אנוס, while an ordinary מפקיר נזקיו is liable.

steps.title: A new dispute about giving up ownership of dangerous property
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר argue about מפקיר נזקיו. One says liable and one says exempt, and the following steps work out who holds which view.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: about a person who gives up ownership of his dangerous property, רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר disagree. One says he is liable, and one says he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new מחלוקת between two אמוראים about someone who declares his dangerous property הפקר. It does not yet say which אמורא holds which side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 already said that, in general, one who abandons his dangerous property is liable. Now we learn that this is actually an open argument between רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר. The rest of the sugya will try to connect it to the משנה and work out who says what.

keyTerms.meaning: One who gives up ownership of things of his that cause damage

phrases.english: It was stated: one who renounces ownership of his damaging property;
Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree:
one said: he is liable,
and one said: he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the general rule from step 4 and shows that it is really an argument between אמוראים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a מחלוקת between רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר whether מפקיר נזקיו is liable or exempt.

steps.title: Suggesting the dispute matches רבי מאיר and the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the one who says liable follows רבי מאיר and the one who says exempt follows the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that the one who holds liable follows רבי מאיר, and the one who holds exempt follows the רבנן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes a suggestion: maybe these two אמוראים are just repeating the older argument between רבי מאיר and the רבנן. This prepares the next step, which will answer the suggestion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier we saw that רבי מאיר holds a stumbler liable and the רבנן exempt him. The simple idea is that this is the same argument as מפקיר נזקיו. If so, each אמורא would just be siding with one תנא.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? It introduces a suggestion the גמרא will test
The one who holds him liable
The one who holds him exempt

phrases.english: Shall we say the one who deems him liable holds like Rabbi Meir,
and the one who deems him exempt holds like the Rabbis?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to link the new מחלוקת from step 5 to the older תנאים argument.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the אמוראים' argument just the same as the argument between רבי מאיר and the רבנן?

steps.title: Everyone agrees with רבי מאיר; they argue about the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: The suggestion is rejected. According to רבי מאיר, all agree he is liable. The argument is only how to read the רבנן: the one who says liable explains that the רבנן exempt only in the משנה's case, because the person was an אנוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבי מאיר, everyone agrees that he is liable. They argue only about the opinion of the רבנן. The one who says exempt follows the רבנן as they sound. The one who says liable can tell you: 'I say this even according to the רבנן. The רבנן exempt only the case here, because the person was an אנוס, someone who could not help what happened. But in a normal case of giving up ownership of dangerous property, they hold him liable.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Both אמוראים can fit the רבנן, so the argument is not simply רבי מאיר against the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody argues against רבי מאיר: if a stumbler is liable, surely someone who chooses to make his property הפקר is liable. The question is why the רבנן exempt. One side says it is because the property is now הפקר. The other side says it is only because he was an אנוס, so a normal הפקר stays liable. This is the same idea as רבי יוחנן's lesson in step 4.

keyTerms.meaning: Only in this case do they say it, and not in others
Someone forced by circumstances he could not control
In general; a normal, ordinary case

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the רבנן hold that a person who makes his property הפקר is always exempt. According to the one who says liable, the רבנן exempt only because the stumbler was an אנוס.

phrases.english: According to Rabbi Meir,
everyone agrees that he is liable,
when they disagree, it is about the opinion of the Rabbis.
The one who deems him exempt follows the Rabbis;
and the one who deems him liable will say to you:
What I said holds even according to the Rabbis,
the Rabbis exempt only
in the case of renouncing damaging property here,
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the case in our משנה, where the person stumbled and fell.

phrases.english: because he is a victim of circumstances;
but in a general case of renouncing damaging property, they deem him liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 6 and moves the argument to the view of the רבנן alone.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the אמוראים are just following רבי מאיר and the רבנן.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The suggestion assumed the רבנן's exemption comes from הפקר. It could instead come only from the fact that he was an אנוס.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the רבנן's exemption in the משנה is a special case of an אנוס, not a general rule that הפקר removes liability.

steps.title: Proof that רבי אלעזר is the one who says liable
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר taught in the name of רבי ישמעאל that a pit in the public domain is treated as the person's own, even though it is not. So he would also hold מפקיר נזקיו liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: We can conclude that רבי אלעזר is the one who says liable. For רבי אלעזר said in the name of רבי ישמעאל: two things are not in a person's possession, yet the פסוק treats them as if they were. They are a pit in the public domain, and חמץ from the sixth hour onward.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to figure out which אמורא holds 'liable'. It brings a teaching of רבי אלעזר that points to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בור dug in public ground does not belong to the digger, yet the תורה still makes him liable as if it were his. The same goes for חמץ after midday on ערב פסח: it is forbidden to benefit from, yet it still counts as his for the מצוה to destroy it. If רבי אלעזר holds that the תורה treats something that is not yours as yours, he would surely hold that a person who makes his dangerous property הפקר is still liable.

keyTerms.meaning: It may be concluded; we can prove who said which view
A pit dug in the public domain

phrases.aramaic: תִּסְתַּיֵּים דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר הוּא דְּאָמַר חַיָּיב –
phrases.english: It may be concluded that Rabbi Elazar is the one who said liable,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל:
phrases.english: as Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Yishmael:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁנֵי דְּבָרִים אֵינָן בִּרְשׁוּתוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם,
phrases.english: Two things are not in a person's possession,
yet the verse made them as if they were in his possession;
and these are: a pit in the public domain,
and chametz from six hours onward.
phrases.notes: Six hours means midday on ערב פסח. After that it is forbidden to benefit from the חמץ, but it still counts as his.

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּסְתַּיֵּים דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר הוּא דְּאָמַר חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining the argument, the גמרא now works out which אמורא holds which view.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי אלעזר holds מפקיר נזקיו is liable
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אלעזר in the name of רבי ישמעאל: a pit in the public domain and חמץ after six hours are treated as the person's own

steps.title: The proof is accepted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the proof: רבי אלעזר says liable, so רבי יוחנן says exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Indeed, it may be concluded.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the proof and does not challenge it. So רבי אלעזר is the one who holds מפקיר נזקיו liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the proof stands, רבי אלעזר is now taken to be the one who says liable. That would leave רבי יוחנן as the one who says exempt, which the גמרא states openly in step 18. The repeated word תסתיים is the גמרא's way of saying the proof works.
steps.whatToRemember: For now, the proof shows רבי אלעזר says a מפקיר נזקיו is liable, based on his teaching that a בור in public ground is treated as his. Both אמוראים agree with רבי מאיר and argue only about why the רבנן exempt the stumbler. This assignment is challenged right away in step 10, and step 23 later decides that רבי יוחנן is really the one who says liable.

phrases.english: Indeed, it may be concluded.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Confirms the proof brought in step 8.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי אלעזר holds that one who renounces ownership of his dangerous property is liable, and רבי יוחנן holds he is exempt.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר seems to say the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the conclusion that רבי אלעזר holds מפקיר נזקיו liable. It quotes his comment on a משנה about turning over dung, which suggests he holds the opposite.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי אלעזר really say this? He said the opposite! The משנה teaches that if someone turns over dung in the public domain and another person is hurt by it, he is liable. רבי אלעזר said: this is only when he meant to acquire the dung. If he did not mean to acquire it, he is exempt. So it seems that in his view מפקיר נזקיו is exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the conclusion of step 9 by pointing to another statement of רבי אלעזר that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 9 we decided that רבי אלעזר says a person stays liable for a hazard he gave up ownership of. But here he says a person who handled dung is exempt if he did not intend to own it. Not owning it sounds just like מפקיר נזקיו, so it looks like he holds 'exempt'.

keyTerms.meaning: To acquire them, to take ownership

phrases.english: And did Rabbi Elazar really say this?
phrases.notes: 'This' means what we just concluded in step 9: that מפקיר נזקיו is liable.

phrases.english: But Rabbi Elazar said the opposite!
As we learned in a משנה:
One who turns over dung in the public domain,
and someone else was hurt by it, is liable for his damage.
And Rabbi Elazar said: They only taught this
where he intended to acquire it,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל לֹא נִתְכַּוֵּין לִזְכּוֹת בָּהֶן – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: but if he did not intend to acquire it, he is exempt.
So apparently, one who gives up ownership of his hazards is exempt!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר הָכִי? וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אִיפְּכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of step 9 that רבי אלעזר holds 'liable'.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion that רבי אלעזר holds מפקיר נזקיו liable.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אלעזר exempts the one who turns over dung without intending to acquire it. Not owning a hazard is the same idea as מפקיר נזקיו, so he must hold 'exempt'.

steps.title: He put the dung back where it was
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה answers that רבי אלעזר's exemption is only where the person returned the dung to its original spot.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said: רבי אלעזר is talking about a case where he put the dung back in its place.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא בר אהבה limits רבי אלעזר's exemption to a specific case, so it no longer contradicts what we said in step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the person moved the dung to a new spot, he created a new hazard and is liable even without intending to own it. Only when he put it back where it already was did he add nothing, so he is liable only if he meant to acquire it. So the dung ruling is not about מפקיר נזקיו at all, and the contradiction goes away.

keyTerms.meaning: He returned it to its place

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said:
It is where he put it back in its place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 10.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אלעזר exempts anyone who handles dung without intending to own it, which would mean מפקיר נזקיו is exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption applies only when the dung was put back in its original place, so no new hazard was created. It says nothing about מפקיר נזקיו.

steps.title: רבינא's comparison: covering and uncovering a pit
steps.stepSummary: רבינא explains רב אדא בר אהבה's answer with a comparison: someone who finds an open pit, covers it, then uncovers it again.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Here is a comparison for רב אדא בר אהבה's answer. It is like someone who finds an uncovered pit, covers it, and then uncovers it again.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives a picture to help us understand why putting the dung back in place makes the person exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If you cover someone else's open pit and then uncover it, you only left things the way you found them. The pit is still the first digger's responsibility. In the same way, putting the dung back is just leaving it as it was.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
A comparison for Rav Adda bar Ahava's answer:
What is it like?
Like one who finds an uncovered pit,
and covered it, and then uncovered it again.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָשָׁל דְּרַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה לָמָּה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports and explains the answer of step 11 with a comparison.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It is not clear why putting the dung back should be different from moving it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Putting it back is like covering a pit and uncovering it: you only restored what was already there, so you are exempt.

steps.title: מר זוטרא: the comparison does not fit
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא challenges רבינא's comparison. With the covered pit the first hazard never went away, but with the dung the first hazard was removed when it was moved.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא son of רב מרי said to רבינא: Are these really alike? There, with the pit, the first act was never undone. Here, with the dung, the first act was undone.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא says רבינא's comparison is wrong because the two cases are different in a key way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Covering a pit does not get rid of the pit; the hole is still there, so the original digger is still responsible. But picking up the dung really removed the hazard from that spot. So putting it back creates the hazard all over again.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מָרִי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Mari, said to Ravina:
Are they really alike?!

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם – לָא אִסְתַּלֻּק לְהוּ מַעֲשֵׂה רִאשׁוֹן,
phrases.english: There, the first act was not removed,
phrases.notes: 'There' is the pit. Covering it did not fill the hole, so the original digging is still in place.

phrases.english: here, the first act was removed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבינא's comparison in step 12.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבינא's comparison of the dung to covering and uncovering a pit.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: With the pit the original hazard stayed in place, but moving the dung fully removed the original hazard.

steps.title: The right comparison: filling and re-digging a pit
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא gives the comparison he thinks is correct. Returning the dung is like filling an open pit and digging it again, which makes the pit his and makes him liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is only like someone who finds an uncovered pit, fills it in, and then digs it out again. There the first act was removed, and the pit now stands as his own.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא finishes his point by giving the comparison that really fits the dung case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Filling the pit ended the first digger's hazard, so digging it again makes a brand-new pit that belongs to the second person, and he is liable. The same is true of the dung: putting it back makes a new hazard. So even in רב אדא בר אהבה's case the person should be liable, and the answer of step 11 is in trouble.

keyTerms.meaning: And it stands in his possession (it is his responsibility)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think מר זוטרא is just making a side point about pits. His comparison means that putting the dung back should make a person liable, which weakens רב אדא בר אהבה's answer to the contradiction.

phrases.english: This is only like
one who finds an uncovered pit,
and filled it in, and then dug it out again,
where the first act was removed,
and it now stands in his possession!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא לָא דָּמֵי אֶלָּא לְמוֹצֵא בּוֹר מְגוּלָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes מר זוטרא's challenge from step 13 by giving the correct comparison.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that putting the dung back leaves the person exempt, and with it רב אדא בר אהבה's answer.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Once the first hazard is removed, putting it back creates a new hazard that belongs to him, like re-digging a filled pit.

steps.title: רב אשי: The dung was turned over below three handbreadths
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a new answer to the קשיא from רבי אלעזר's comment on the dung משנה. The case is one where the person turned the dung over less than three טפחים from the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אשי said: it is talking about where he turned it over less than three טפחים from the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא knocked out the earlier answer, so רב אשי offers a different way to explain רבי אלעזר's exemption.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the dung never went three טפחים up, it was never really lifted, so it was never taken out of its original place. It becomes the new person's only if he meant to acquire it. So when רבי אלעזר says 'exempt' without that intent, he is not saying a person who gives up his hazard is exempt. He is saying the hazard was never this person's to begin with.

keyTerms.meaning: less than three טפחים off the ground

steps.confusionAlert: Turning something over below three טפחים is not a halachic 'lifting'. The object is treated as if it never left its place.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ashi said:
When he turned it over less than three [handbreadths].
phrases.notes: "Three" means three טפחים off the ground. Below that, it doesn't count as really lifting it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב אדא בר אהבה's answer, which מר זוטרא rejected
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אלעזר's exemption seemed to mean that one who gives up his hazard is exempt
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption is only because dung turned over below three never became his without intent to acquire it

steps.title: Why did רבי אלעזר pick the narrow below-three case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי אלעזר set the משנה in a case below three טפחים, where liability depends on intent. He could have set it above three, where the person is liable even without intent.
steps.simpleTranslation: What pushed רבי אלעזר to explain the משנה as turning it over less than three, so that he is liable only because he meant to acquire it, and without that intent he is not? He should explain it as above three, and then he is liable even if he did not mean to acquire it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אשי's reading. It asks why רבי אלעזר would explain the משנה in such a limited way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lifting above three is a full lifting, so the dung becomes his responsibility even without intent. That reading would make the משנה's ruling of liability simple. Choosing the narrow below-three case looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: to set it in a specific case

phrases.english: And what forced Rabbi Elazar
to explain it as a case where he turned it over less than three,
so that the reason [he is liable] is that he intended to acquire it,

phrases.aramaic: הָא אֵין מִתְכַּוֵּין לִזְכּוֹת בָּהּ – לָא?
phrases.english: but if he does not intend to acquire it, not?
Let him explain it as above three,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא נִתְכַּוֵּין לִזְכּוֹת בָּהּ – חַיָּיב!
phrases.english: and then even though he did not intend to acquire it, he is liable!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's reading of רבי אלעזר
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's choice to set the משנה below three טפחים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A simpler reading exists (above three, liable with no intent needed), so why choose the narrow one?

steps.title: רבא: The word 'turned over' means below three
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the wording of the משנה forced רבי אלעזר. The משנה says הפך (turned over), not הגביה (lifted), so it must mean below three טפחים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: the משנה was difficult for him. Why does it say 'turned over'? It should say 'lifted'! So learn from this that 'turned over' always means below three.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question. The משנה's own choice of words pushed רבי אלעזר to the below-three case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה meant a full lifting, it would have used the word 'lifted'. Since it chose 'turned over', it is describing a low movement, under three טפחים. In that case only intent to acquire makes him responsible, which is exactly what רבי אלעזר said.

phrases.english: Rava said: The mishna was difficult for him.
Why does it say specifically "turned over"?
Let it teach "lifted"!
Rather, learn from it:
every "turned over" is below three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16
steps.terutzResolutionType: Precise reading of the משנה's wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אלעזר could have explained the משנה as above three
steps.terutzMaskana: The word הפך shows the משנה is talking about below three

steps.title: Conclusion: רבי אלעזר says liable, so רבי יוחנן says exempt
steps.stepSummary: With the problem solved, the גמרא concludes that רבי אלעזר holds מפקיר נזקיו חייב. That means רבי יוחנן is the one who holds פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since רבי אלעזר is the one who said liable, רבי יוחנן is the one who said exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the question of who said what. רבי אלעזר says liable, so רבי יוחנן says exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר's comment on the dung משנה no longer contradicts the view that he holds liable. So the earlier dispute can be assigned: חייב is רבי אלעזר and פטור is רבי יוחנן.
steps.whatToRemember: At this point the גמרא assigns the views this way: רבי אלעזר says חייב and רבי יוחנן says פטור. The very next steps challenge רבי יוחנן's side, and step 23 reverses it.

phrases.english: And since Rabbi Elazar said liable,
Rabbi Yochanan said exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the final conclusion now that the challenge of step 10 is resolved
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: מפקיר נזקיו: רבי אלעזר says חייב, רבי יוחנן says פטור

steps.title: Challenge from the thorn-fence משנה and רבי יוחנן's comment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether רבי יוחנן really holds פטור. It quotes a משנה about thorns, glass and fences that harm people, and רבי יוחנן's comment that the thorn fence makes a person liable only when the thorns stick out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי יוחנן really say this? We learned in a משנה: if someone hides a thorn or glass, or makes a fence of thorns, or his fence fell into the public area, and someone got hurt, he must pay. And רבי יוחנן said: this is only when the thorns stick out, but if he keeps them inside his own space, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a challenge against the idea that רבי יוחנן holds מפקיר נזקיו פטור. It sets up the sources: a משנה and רבי יוחנן's comment on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is proven yet. The גמרא is laying out the source: רבי יוחנן limits the thorn-fence liability to a case where the thorns stick out (מפריח), and he exempts a case where they stay inside (מצמצם). The next step will draw the inference.

keyTerms.meaning: One who hides or tucks away an object
Sticks out, here meaning the thorns stick out into the public area
Keeps inside, here meaning the thorns stay within his own property
They only taught this in the case of

phrases.english: And did Rabbi Yochanan really say this?!

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתְנַן: הַמַּצְנִיעַ אֶת הַקּוֹץ וְאֶת הַזְּכוּכִית;
phrases.english: But didn't we learn: one who hides a thorn or glass;
or one who builds his fence with thorns;
or a fence that fell into the public domain;
and another person was hurt by them, he is liable for his damage.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּמַפְרִיחַ,
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said: they taught this only where he makes the thorns stick out,
but where he keeps them inside, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הָכִי?! וְהָתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of step 18 that רבי יוחנן holds מפקיר נזקיו פטור.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יוחנן holds מפקיר נזקיו פטור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן's own comment on the thorn-fence משנה will be used to show he holds חייב.

steps.title: Inference that רבי יוחנן holds the owner liable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reasons that the inside-thorns case is exempt because it counts as a pit on his own property. So pit liability must apply in the public area, which he does not own. That means מפקיר נזקיו חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why is the inside case exempt? Isn't it because it is a pit on his own property? That shows the liability for a pit is in the public area. So a person who gives up ownership of his damaging things is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the challenge by drawing an inference from רבי יוחנן's comment. It concludes that רבי יוחנן holds מפקיר נזקיו חייב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic goes: inside his own property it is exempt, so the liability must come from the public area. But a pit in the public area does not belong to him, so his liability there means that even ownerless damaging things make him liable. This goes against what step 18 said about רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: A pit on his own property
One who gives up ownership of his damaging things

phrases.english: Where he keeps them inside, why is he exempt?

phrases.aramaic: לָאו מִשּׁוּם דְּהָוְיָא לֵיהּ בּוֹר בִּרְשׁוּתוֹ?
phrases.english: Is it not because it is a pit on his own property?

phrases.aramaic: מִכְּלַל דְּחִיּוּבָא דְבוֹר – בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים הוּא;
phrases.english: This shows that the liability for a pit is in the public domain;
phrases.notes: A pit in the public area doesn't belong to him, so being liable there means being liable for something he doesn't own.

phrases.english: So apparently, one who gives up ownership of his damaging things is liable!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the sources quoted in step 19, completing the challenge.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יוחנן holds מפקיר נזקיו חייב.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's exemption of מצמצם in the thorn-fence משנה, explained as a pit on his own property.

steps.title: A different reason the inside-thorns case is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יוחנן can still hold פטור. The inside case is exempt for a different reason given by רב אחא בריה דרב איקא: people do not usually rub against walls.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, really I can tell you that one who gives up ownership of his damaging things is exempt. And why is the inside case exempt? Because רב אחא son of רב איקא said about it: people do not usually rub against walls.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the inference and keeps רבי יוחנן's view as פטור. It explains the inside-thorns exemption in a different way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge depended on the reason "it is a pit on his own property." The answer replaces that reason: the inside case is exempt because getting hurt by rubbing against a wall is not normal behavior. So nothing can be learned about pit liability from that case.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, I can tell you (keeping the original position)
For it was said about this case

steps.confusionAlert: The answer does not say the inside thorns are a pit on his property at all. It gives a completely different reason: people don't normally brush against walls.

phrases.english: No, really I can tell you:
one who gives up ownership of his damaging things is exempt;
and where he keeps them inside, why is he exempt?
Because it was said about it,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha son of Rav Ika said:

phrases.aramaic: לְפִי שֶׁאֵין דַּרְכָּן שֶׁל בְּנֵי אָדָם
phrases.english: because it is not the way of people
to rub against walls.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 19 and 20 by replacing the reason behind the מצמצם exemption.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a different reason for the source, so the inference no longer follows.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The inside case is exempt because it is a pit on his own property, which would show that pit liability applies even to ownerless pits in the public area.
steps.terutzMaskana: The inside case is exempt because people don't normally rub against walls, so רבי יוחנן can still hold מפקיר נזקיו פטור.

steps.title: Challenge from the unnamed משנה about a pit in the public area
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: רבי יוחנן rules that the הלכה follows an unnamed משנה, and an unnamed משנה says one who digs a pit in the public area is liable when an animal falls in and dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי יוחנן really say this? But רבי יוחנן said the הלכה follows an unnamed משנה, and we learned: one who digs a pit in the public area, and an ox or donkey fell in and died, is liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a second challenge against the idea that רבי יוחנן holds מפקיר נזקיו פטור. The next step accepts this challenge and changes which view רבי יוחנן holds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pit in the public area does not belong to the person who dug it, yet the משנה makes him liable. Since רבי יוחנן follows unnamed משניות, he should hold מפקיר נזקיו חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: The הלכה follows a משנה that states a law without naming who said it

steps.whyThisMatters: This challenge uses a general rule of רבי יוחנן about how to decide הלכה, so it is harder to push aside than a single comment.

phrases.english: And did Rabbi Yochanan really say this?
But didn't Rabbi Yochanan say:
the halacha follows an unnamed Mishnah,
and we learned: one who digs a pit in the public domain,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר וָמֵת – חַיָּיב!
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, is liable!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הָכִי? וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first challenge was answered, the גמרא brings a new challenge against the same position.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יוחנן holds מפקיר נזקיו פטור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן follows unnamed משניות, and an unnamed משנה makes the digger liable for a pit in the public area, which he does not own.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן really holds liable
steps.stepSummary: Because of the challenge from the unnamed משנה, the גמרא reverses itself. It concludes that רבי יוחנן is the one who says מפקיר נזקיו חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, really, רבי יוחנן is the one who said 'liable.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the challenge from Step 22 and flips its earlier conclusion. Now רבי יוחנן is the one who says a person who gives up ownership of his dangerous things is still liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 18 the גמרא said רבי אלעזר holds חייב, so רבי יוחנן must hold פטור. But רבי יוחנן rules like an unnamed משנה, and that משנה makes a person liable for a pit in the public area, which he does not own. So the גמרא now says רבי יוחנן holds חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; signals dropping the earlier idea
Really, actually; this is the true position
One who gives up ownership of his dangerous objects

steps.whatToRemember: The positions are now switched: רבי יוחנן holds מפקיר נזקיו חייב.
steps.confusionAlert: This is the opposite of Step 18. The earlier conclusion is dropped, so don't mix up who holds what.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how one source, an unnamed משנה that רבי יוחנן follows, can force the גמרא to change which אמורא holds which opinion.

phrases.english: Rather, actually,
phrases.notes: This means: forget what we said in Step 18. Here is the true picture.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of Step 22 and reverses the conclusion of Step 18.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יוחנן holds that one who gives up ownership of his dangerous objects is חייב.

steps.title: Does that mean רבי אלעזר holds exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether it follows that רבי אלעזר holds פטור, and begins to bring a statement of רבי אלעזר that seems to show otherwise.
steps.simpleTranslation: And just because רבי יוחנן said 'liable,' does that mean רבי אלעזר said 'exempt'? But didn't רבי אלעזר say...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new challenge. It questions the idea that רבי אלעזר must hold פטור and starts to quote him. The actual quote comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, the assumption was that the two אמוראים disagree, so if one says חייב the other must say פטור. The גמרא now doubts this. It is about to bring a statement where רבי אלעזר seems to hold חייב too.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt, does not have to pay
But didn't he say? Introduces a contradicting statement

phrases.english: And from the fact that Rabbi Yoḥanan said liable,
does it follow that Rabbi Elazar said exempt?!
But didn't Rabbi Elazar say

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִדְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר חַיָּיב רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר פָּטוּר וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions what follows from Step 23's new conclusion about רבי אלעזר's opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that רבי אלעזר holds מפקיר נזקיו פטור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A statement of רבי אלעזר, about to be quoted, appears to make him hold חייב as well, so he cannot simply be the one who says פטור.
